anchor_text: wanting guilders to redeem their lives
summary: 'Guilders' are gold coins, originally Dutch (from 'gulden', meaning golden). The Duke says Syracusan merchants who lacked the money to pay the ransom — a thousand marks — have paid with their lives instead, dying under the law. 'Wanting' here means lacking, not desiring.
detail: The guilder was a gold coin widely familiar in Elizabethan England through trade with the Netherlands. Its use here establishes the play's commercial world — the city of Ephesus is above all a trading port, and the conflict between Syracuse and Ephesus is an economic quarrel as well as a political one. The detail that merchants 'seal'd his rigorous statutes with their bloods' (line 9) means they paid the death penalty when they could not pay the cash ransom.

anchor_text: mortal and intestine jars
summary: 'Intestine jars' means internal conflicts or quarrels — civil strife within a nation, not between foreign enemies. 'Jars' here means discords or disputes, and 'intestine' means inward, domestic. The Duke is saying that the bloody feuding between Ephesus and Syracuse is a deep, ongoing civil-political enmity, not merely a recent incident.
detail: Both words are now archaic in these senses. 'Intestine' derives from Latin intestinus (inward, internal) and was standard Elizabethan political vocabulary for civil war or domestic conflict — compare 'intestine shock / And furious close of civil butchery' in 1 Henry IV. 'Jars' meaning quarrels or discords survives in the phrase 'jarring notes.' The legal framing of the scene — decrees, synods, statutes, penalty, ransom — establishes Ephesus as a city governed by rigorous commercial law.

anchor_text: admit no traffic to our adverse towns
summary: 'Traffic' means trade or commercial exchange, not road vehicles. 'Adverse' means hostile or enemy. The decree forbids any commercial dealings between Ephesus and Syracuse — a trade embargo backed by death. This is the law that has condemned Aegeon.
detail: The trade-war framing is essential context: Aegeon is not a spy or criminal but a merchant who wandered into a hostile port while searching for his son. The word 'traffic' in Shakespeare almost always means trade or commerce (compare 'traffickers' in The Merchant of Venice). 'Adverse towns' means enemy cities, treating Syracuse and Ephesus as opposing city-states in a commercial cold war.

anchor_text: a thousand marks be levied
summary: A 'mark' was a unit of money worth two-thirds of a pound sterling (13 shillings 4 pence). A thousand marks was therefore a very large sum — roughly the annual wage of a prosperous craftsman multiplied many times over. Aegeon's entire estate comes to less than a hundred marks, making the ransom impossible. The gap sets up the play's opening despair.
detail: The mark was never a coin in England but a unit of account, derived from a weight of silver. Shakespeare uses marks as a general measure of substantial sums throughout his plays. The detail that Aegeon cannot raise even a tenth of the required ransom means the Duke's offer of a day's reprieve is a mercy with no real hope attached — or so it seems until his lost family turns out to be in Ephesus all along.

anchor_text: To Epidamnum, till my factor's death
summary: Epidamnum (modern Durres, Albania) was a port city on the eastern Adriatic, a standard setting in Roman comedy for merchant adventures and misadventures. A 'factor' was a commercial agent — someone who bought and sold goods on behalf of a merchant employer. Aegeon was drawn away from home by business when his factor died and left his goods unprotected.
detail: In Plautus's Menaechmi — the principal source for The Comedy of Errors — Epidamnus (the Latin form) is where the story takes place. Shakespeare moves the main action to Ephesus, but retains Epidamnum as the port Aegeon traded with. The death of a factor leaving goods 'at random' (TLN 43: unprotected, at risk) was a realistic commercial hazard for Elizabethan merchants who relied on agents abroad. The word 'factor' is now almost obsolete in this sense; a modern equivalent would be a local broker or agent.

Aegeon uses the phrasing to avoid direct mention of pregnancy while making the audience understand that his wife was heavily pregnant when she followed him to Epidamnum.

summary: This is the foundational premise of the whole comedy: Aegeon's twin sons were indistinguishable by sight and had to be told apart by name. Shakespeare doubles this by also giving each master a servant twin (the two Dromios), making four indistinguishable people in two pairs.

anchor_text: for their parents were exceeding poor,-- / I bought
summary: Aegeon purchased the second pair of twin boys — the future Dromios — because their parents were too poor to keep them. This makes the Dromios bondmen (slaves). In the Roman comedies that are Shakespeare's source, the comic servants are explicitly slaves; Shakespeare softens the word to 'bondman' but preserves the legal status. The twins' bond of servitude explains why they cannot simply walk away from the errors that torment them throughout the play.
detail: In Plautus the servus (slave) figure was the stock comedian and schemer of Roman comedy. Shakespeare inherits the type as the clown-servant Dromio, but the Elizabethan context is ambiguous: English law did not permit outright domestic slavery, so the word 'bondman' or 'bondservant' carried overtones of contracted indenture or apprenticeship as well as ancient servitude. The Dromios are beaten repeatedly by masters who are not even their own masters — a routine comic convention in Plautine farce that could feel more brutal on a modern stage.

anchor_text: the always-wind-obeying deep
summary: A compressed, hyphenated compound adjective describing the sea as something that simply obeys whatever wind blows upon it — indifferent and ungovernable. Aegeon is contrasting the sea's amoral obedience with the human need for safety. The phrasing also signals that the shipwreck was not caused by the sea's malice but by the sheer force of circumstance.
detail: The phrase is an example of the Shakespearean habit of coining compound epithets to pack a complex idea into a noun modifier. The underlying idea — that the sea obeys the wind and the wind obeys no human will — was a commonplace of classical navigation poetry (compare Ovid, Tristia 1.2 on the helplessness of sailors in a storm). The whole shipwreck narrative (TLN 63-121) is deliberately modelled on classical epic storm-and-separation episodes (Virgil, Aeneid 1; Ovid, Metamorphoses 11) and establishes Aegeon as a figure of tragic stature in what will become a comedy.

anchor_text: more careful for the latter-born, / Had fast'ned him unto a small spare mast
summary: Aegeon's wife lashes one set of twins to a mast — one twin + one servant — and he holds the other. This is how the family is split: when the ship breaks apart, each half drifts separately. The 'latter-born' twin is the younger son (who in the play becomes Antipholus of Ephesus, raised by strangers in Corinth and eventually adopted by the Duke's patron). The detail explains why the twins were separated and why neither knows the other survived.
detail: Elizabethan audiences would have recognized shipwreck-and-separation as a romance convention, familiar from Greek prose romances such as Heliodorus's Aethiopica (translated into English 1569) and from Plautus's expository prologues. The specific mast-and-storm separation, however, is Shakespeare's own dramatic invention: in Plautus's Menaechmi the twins are parted not by shipwreck but when one is lost at a festival in Tarentum. What Shakespeare takes from Plautus is the underlying framework — identical twins separated in childhood, each unaware the other lives — onto which he grafts the storm. The 'spare mast' detail is nautically plausible: spare spars were carried as emergency floating aids. The scene sets up the play's deepest structural irony — the final-scene reunion is possible only because of the very wreck that destroyed the family.

anchor_text: in this unjust divorce of us / Fortune had left to both of us alike
summary: Aegeon calls the shipwreck splitting his family an 'unjust divorce' — a legal term borrowed for a natural catastrophe. Divorce in Elizabethan usage meant any forcible separation, not only the dissolving of a marriage. Fortune here is personified as a callous deity who has arranged the disaster 'justly' by giving each half of the family one child and one servant — a grim equality.
detail: The word 'Fortune' appears here in its classical personification as a goddess who distributes fate arbitrarily. Boethius's image of Fortune's wheel (Consolatio Philosophiae II) was the standard Renaissance framework for this kind of reversal: from prosperity (voyages, wealth, good sons) to ruin (storm, separation, poverty, the sentence of death). Aegeon's narrative — a prosperous merchant destroyed by Fortune — is a de casibus pattern embedded in a comedy, creating the unusual tonal register of this opening scene, which reads more like tragedy than farce.

anchor_text: Five summers have I spent in furthest Greece, / Roaming clean through the bounds of Asia, / And, coasting homeward, came to Ephesus
summary: Aegeon has spent five years searching across the ancient Greek world and through Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), heading toward home — and arrived at Ephesus. Ephesus was a major port city on the Aegean coast of Asia Minor, part of what is now western Turkey. His journey explains why a Syracusan ends up condemned in Ephesus, and sets the play's geography: Syracuse in Sicily, the Adriatic, the Aegean, and Asia.
detail: The geography is loosely Mediterranean: 'furthest Greece' and 'the bounds of Asia' suggest the eastern Aegean and Anatolia. Ephesus itself (modern Selcuk in Turkey) was a real and famous ancient city — a major centre of Greek culture, Roman administration, and early Christianity, best known to Elizabethan audiences from Acts 19 (St Paul's mission there and the riot of the silversmiths of Diana of the Ephesians). Shakespeare's choice of Ephesus, rather than Plautus's Epidamnus, is freighted with these biblical and magical associations.

anchor_text: give out you are of Epidamnum
summary: The Merchant warns Antipholus of Syracuse to pretend he is from Epidamnum, not Syracuse, because a Syracusan merchant has just been arrested and faces execution under Ephesus's law against enemy nationals (established in 1.1). Antipholus is in the same danger and must conceal his identity — the irony being that the play will hinge on his identity being constantly mistaken by others.
detail: The law is taken from Plautus's Menaechmi, which is set in Epidamnus (Shakespeare uses both forms of the name). In the source, however, it is mainly a framing device; Shakespeare expands it into the Aegeon plot, giving the life-or-death stakes of the law human weight by making the condemned merchant Aegeon the lost father of the very twins whose confusions drive the farce. The audience knows this from 1.1; Antipholus does not. 'Give out' means 'declare publicly,' 'spread the word that.'

anchor_text: bear it to the Centaur, where we host
summary: The Centaur is the name of the inn where Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio are staying. Elizabethan inns commonly took their names from heraldic badges or mythological creatures — the Centaur (a half-man, half-horse creature of Greek myth) was a real inn-sign type. 'Where we host' means 'where we are lodging.' The money he tells Dromio to take there is the gold that will soon go missing.
detail: Centaurs in classical mythology were notorious for unruly, drunken behaviour — most famously at the Lapiths' wedding feast, where they brawled and attempted to carry off the women (Ovid, Metamorphoses 12.210-535). The inn-name carries a faint comic charge for a scene about disorder and misidentification. The other inn named in the play, the Phoenix (TLN 234), is the house of Antipholus of Ephesus, so the audience has two competing 'homes' for men with the same name and face.

anchor_text: I to the world am like a drop of water
summary: Antipholus of Syracuse describes his search for his lost family with an extended simile: he is a drop of water trying to find another drop in the ocean — which, if it fails, is absorbed and lost, unseen and unindividuated. The image captures both his quest ('to find a mother and a brother') and his fear that in searching he will lose himself entirely. This is one of the play's few moments of genuine emotional depth amid the farce.
detail: The conceit is a compressed simile that runs four lines before its application ('So I'). The logic is precise: a drop seeking its fellow in the ocean has two possible outcomes — reunion or dissolution. Since the drop that 'fails to find his fellow forth' is '(Unseen, inquisitive)' it undergoes a kind of death-in-life, existing without identity. The word 'confounds' carries both senses at once — 'loses itself' (blends indistinguishably) and 'destroys itself.' The fear of losing one's sense of self is thematically central to the play: Antipholus of Syracuse, newly arrived in a city he believes full of sorcery, is about to be swept into a day in which everyone treats him as a man he is not. The soliloquy is the play's emotional manifesto before the farce machine starts.

anchor_text: Here comes the almanac of my true date
summary: Antipholus of Syracuse sees Dromio of Ephesus enter — but thinks it is his own Dromio of Syracuse — and calls him 'the almanac of my true date,' meaning 'a living calendar that records my real age.' Because they were born the same day to the same parents (Dromio S is the twin of Dromio E), seeing Dromio confirms Antipholus's own birth-date as surely as an almanac confirms the calendar. The joke is that the Dromio arriving is the wrong one — the first instance of the play's central engine: a character correctly identifying someone and being completely wrong.
detail: An almanac was a yearly calendar giving dates, feast days, and astrological data; it was the Elizabethan equivalent of a wall planner. The conceit is exact: if the twins share a birthday, each Dromio is, to his master, a human timestamp. The audience already knows from 1.1 that both pairs of twins were born on the same day. Antipholus's use of 'true' ('my true date') carries the play's central irony: he thinks he is about to confirm a truth and will instead enter a cascade of error.

anchor_text: Return'd so soon! rather approach'd too late
summary: The play's first mistaken-identity collision. The Dromio who enters is Dromio of Ephesus, sent to fetch his own master, Antipholus of Ephesus, home to dinner; he has never met Antipholus of Syracuse. The Syracusan, thinking this is his own Dromio (just sent to the Centaur), is baffled that he has 'returned' so quickly — but this Dromio never left. Everything he says (the burning capon, the angry mistress, the dinner) is perfectly true, and perfectly meaningless to a Syracusan who has no wife and no dinner waiting.
detail: The scene is a direct adaptation of the confusion scene in Plautus's Menaechmi (Act 2), where the visiting twin meets the local twin's parasite — though Shakespeare raises the stakes by making the servant a twin too. The comedy depends on both characters being entirely sincere: Dromio of Ephesus really is reporting facts to his real master (or so he believes), and Antipholus of Syracuse really does have no idea what is being talked about. Neither is lying. The double sincerity is what makes the scene not just funny but structurally tight.

anchor_text: A man is master of his liberty
summary: Luciana argues that men are naturally free to come and go as they please, and wives must accept it. anchor_text: nothing situate under heaven's eye
summary: Luciana builds a formal argument from Nature to justify wifely obedience: she surveys three realms — earth, sea, and sky — in turn (beasts, fish, and birds), then crowns the list with Man as master of all three. The irony the comedy exploits is that Luciana delivers this polished logical case in defence of an arrangement she has never personally tested. Shakespeare lets her rhetoric win the formal argument while Adriana's lived experience wins the emotional argument.

anchor_text: 'Tis dinner time' quoth I; 'My gold,' quoth he

anchor_text: That like a football you do spurn me thus
summary: Dromio compares himself to a football kicked back and forth between his two tormentors. summary: 'Every why hath a wherefore' was a proverbial maxim meaning that every question has its answer, or every cause has its reason. The joke is that Dromio is fluent enough in the form to demand logical grounds for his beating, while Antipholus gives him reasons that are circular (I beat you for joking; and again for repeating the joke). anchor_text: bald pate of Father Time himself

anchor_text: May he not do it by fine and recovery

anchor_text: Am I in earth, in heaven, or in hell
summary: Antipholus of Syracuse closes the scene with a genuine expression of metaphysical disorientation. The tricolon 'earth, heaven, or in hell' exhausts the universe's three regions; 'sleeping or waking' and 'mad, or well-advis'd' pair the same impossible alternatives. He does not know which state he is in because everything in Ephesus contradicts his knowledge of reality. His resolution — 'I'll say as they say, and persever so, / And in this mist at all adventures go' — is a pragmatic surrender to the confusion.

'Well-advis'd' means in one's right mind, possessing good judgment. 'Mist' is both literal confusion and a standard metaphor for moral or intellectual darkness; 'at all adventures' means taking whatever chance brings, venturing without a map. The speech is the play's most direct acknowledgment that the farce has real philosophical stakes: identity and sanity are genuinely in question.

anchor_text: thousand marks in gold
summary: A mark was an English and continental unit of account worth two-thirds of a pound sterling (13 shillings and 4 pence). A thousand marks was a very large sum — roughly equivalent to several years' income for a prosperous tradesman. The sum signals that real stakes, not petty change, are at issue.

anchor_text: I have your hand to show

His next two lines extend the conceit: if his skin were parchment (the writing material of legal documents) and the blows were ink, then Antipholus's 'handwriting' — the bruises his fist left — would be his own self-incriminating record. 'Your hand' as signature also carries the literal sense of the fist — the two meanings hinge on a single word, which is the signature of Dromio's punning style throughout.

anchor_text: draw within the compass of suspect
summary: Balthazar urges Antipholus of Ephesus not to force his way into his own house because doing so in broad daylight will drag 'the unviolated honour of your wife' within 'the compass of suspect' — that is, within the range or circle of suspicion. anchor_text: Shall love, in building, grow so ruinate
summary: Luciana is not lecturing the man she thinks is Adriana's husband for being unfaithful; she is urging him to hide it better. Her whole opening speech (TLN 720-747) advises Antipholus of Syracuse — whom she believes to be the Ephesian Antipholus — to dissemble rather than flaunt his straying. The comic complication is that he has never seen Luciana before, so the entire lecture lands on the wrong person.

Because the wrong twin is receiving this advice, the scene doubles as the play's ironic commentary on the marriage-debate thread that runs through Acts 2 and 3.

anchor_text: We in your motion turn, and you may move us
summary: Luciana is drawing on the Ptolemaic model of the cosmos, in which the planets revolve in fixed 'motions' around the earth, each outer sphere carrying the inner ones with it. Women, she says, are like inner planets: they are moved by whatever sphere (man) contains them. The comparison is sincere within the speech but quietly ironic given that she is delivering it to the wrong man.
detail: Elizabethan cosmology held that the heavenly spheres were nested and that each outer sphere imparted its motion downward. In the domestic analogy the husband is the governing sphere and the wife the secondary body that follows. The image completes Luciana's argument from 2.1 (where she told Adriana that a husband is 'master of his liberty' just as the beast is master of his servant), here raised to a cosmic scale. The irony of the scene is that no such orderly planetary motion is on display: the Ephesian Antipholus is shut out of his own house while the Syracusan one is being lectured on submitting to the wife he does not have.

anchor_text: Sweet mistress,--what your name is else, I know not
summary: Antipholus of Syracuse has no idea who Luciana is, which is why he says he does not know her name; she, in turn, has mistaken him for his twin brother Antipholus of Ephesus, Adriana's husband. The whole wooing scene (TLN 748-791) runs on cross-purposes: she thinks she is reproving a straying husband, while he has fallen genuinely in love with a stranger who inexplicably knows his name and treats him as family.

The visiting Antipholus's confusion is sympathetic — he has been addressed all day as someone he is not, and now a beautiful woman who knows his name speaks to him with the intimacy of a sister-in-law. His response ('Are you a god? would you create me new? / Transform me, then, and to your power I'll yield') voices both his bewilderment and genuine attraction. The audience watches two people have an entirely different conversation from the one each thinks is happening — the central mechanism of the Plautine double-identity comedy.

Odysseus had himself lashed to the mast to hear them safely. Antipholus of Syracuse calls Luciana a 'mermaid' and a 'siren' because her voice is drawing him dangerously off course — toward her sister, his supposed wife — but he begs her to sing for herself instead so he can 'dote' on her without drowning.

In Homer (Odyssey 12) the sirens' song promises knowledge; here the danger it poses is specifically that of being pulled toward Adriana (drowning in her 'flood of tears') rather than toward Luciana. The wordplay on 'light' and 'sink' in the next line (TLN 771 — 'Let love, being light, be drowned if she sink!') turns on 'light' meaning both weightless (love will float) and promiscuous/wanton. Antipholus is simultaneously entranced and trying to resist.

anchor_text: Not mad, but mated; how, I do not know
summary: 'Mated' means both 'confounded, bewildered' (the usual Elizabethan sense in the phrase 'checkmate') and 'paired, wedded.' Luciana has just asked if Antipholus of Syracuse is mad; he denies it but says he is 'mated' — dumbfounded by her beauty, and also, perhaps, already half-willing to be matched with her as a partner.

In chess, to be mated is to be left with no move, helpless — which captures Antipholus's condition exactly: he cannot explain anything that is happening to him, cannot leave the city, and now cannot resist the woman speaking to him. The double meaning is confirmed by the courtship that immediately follows (TLN 774-791), where he presses Luciana to acknowledge herself as his 'better part.'

anchor_text: It is thyself, mine own self's better part
summary: Antipholus of Syracuse answers Luciana's 'That's my sister' with the rhetorical figure of the beloved as the other half or better part of the lover's own soul. The convention (drawn from Aristotle's account of friendship in the Nicomachean Ethics: a friend is 'another self') was a standard of Renaissance love poetry — the beloved is described as the lover's soul, eyes, heart, and heaven in quick sequence (TLN 782-785), running the gamut of the Petrarchan blazon.

'Meteors tilting' applies the image of jousting knights to the streaks of light that Elizabethans thought fought one another in the sky; 'tilting' means jousting, and the face is the sky where competing passions — guilt, desire, defiance — clash and are legible to a close observer.
detail: Elizabethan natural philosophy held that meteors, comets, and shooting stars were atmospheric phenomena produced by warm vapours rising from the earth and igniting in the upper air; medical and poetic tradition similarly located the passions in the body's internal 'meteors' of heat and moisture that flushed the face. The conceit works on both registers at once: Adriana is asking, with sharp marital intelligence, whether the betraying blush, pallor, or agitation — the weather of the face — gave her husband away. The irony is that the man Luciana spoke to was not Adriana's husband at all, but his Syracusan twin.

anchor_text: deformed, crooked, old, and sere, Ill-fac'd, worse bodied, shapeless everywhere
summary: Adriana attacks the husband she believes has just courted her own sister. 'Sere' means withered or dried-up — the word for dead leaves or parched vegetation. 'Stigmatical in making' means marked at birth with deformity, as though branded; 'making' = physical form, the way one was made. The outburst is the jealous flip side of love: Adriana demolishes the man she actually loves to assert she does not care.
detail: 'Sere' (Old English sear) was the standard word for dried-out, leafless, or withered; Shakespeare uses it in the Seven Ages of Man ('the lean and slipper'd pantaloon... the sere, the yellow leaf') and elsewhere for physical or emotional depletion. 'Stigmatical' carries a loaded charge: a stigma was literally a brand burned into a slave or criminal, and by extension any mark of disgrace or deformity. Adriana's list — deformed, crooked, old, sere, ill-faced, shapeless, vicious, foolish, blunt, unkind, stigmatical — is a comic blazon in reverse (an anti-blazon), stripping away the conventional praise-of-beauty catalogue. Luciana's cool reply immediately deflates it: if he is so loathsome, why be jealous of him?

anchor_text: Far from her nest the lapwing cries, away
summary: The lapwing (a ground-nesting bird) was proverbial for crying and fluttering far from its nest to lure predators away from its eggs — feigning alarm in the wrong place to protect what it truly cares about. Adriana applies the image to herself: her mouth curses, but her heart prays for him. She is like the lapwing, making noise far from where her real feelings are hidden.
detail: The lapwing's decoy behaviour was so well known in Elizabethan England that it fed a range of proverbial expressions: 'to cry like a lapwing' meant to raise a fuss designed to mislead. The bird appears in several Shakespeare plays for the same idea of deceptive or displaced noise (e.g. Hamlet 5.2, where Osric is a 'lapwing... that ran away with the shell on his head,' meaning a chatterer whose noise means nothing). Here the application is more tender: Adriana recognises she has been speaking against her own love, and the lapwing image is her private, honest acknowledgement of it.

anchor_text: Tartar limbo, worse than hell. A devil in an everlasting garment hath him; One whose hard heart is button'd up with steel
summary: Dromio describes the arresting officer in a cascade of terrifying images. 'Tartar limbo' means the outermost prison of Tartarus — the lowest pit of classical hell — so 'worse than hell' is the hyperbolic claim that a sergeant's custody is hotter than Hades itself. The 'everlasting garment' and 'button'd up with steel' describe the sergeant's buff leather coat, a thick ox-hide jacket worn by officers that resisted a sword-cut and was almost impossible to tear. Elizabethan audiences recognised 'the buff' as immediately as a modern audience would recognise a police uniform.
detail: Tartarus was the deepest abyss of the classical underworld (below even Hades), the place where the worst sinners were confined; 'Tartar' is a common Elizabethan shorthand for it. 'Limbo' in theological usage was the borderland outside hell proper where souls awaited judgment, but in popular speech it meant any place of confinement or detention — here fused with Tartarus for comic extravagance. The buff-leather coat of an arresting officer became so identified with the law that 'buff' or 'a suit of buff' served as metonymy for the sergeant himself, as the wordplay that follows makes clear. The image also touches the play's running Ephesus-as-city-of-sorcery motif: even the plainest legal functionary sounds, in Dromio's description, like a supernatural jailer.

anchor_text: A back-friend, a shoulder-clapper, one that countermands The passages of alleys, creeks, and narrow lands; A hound that runs counter, and yet draws dry foot well
summary: Clues that the man Dromio describes is a sergeant empowered to make arrests. A 'back-friend' is a false friend who stabs you in the back — but also one who claps you on the back to arrest you; a 'shoulder-clapper' is slang for a sergeant, who seized his quarry by tapping the shoulder. 'Countermands the passages of alleys' means he blocks the lanes to cut off escape. 'Runs counter' is a hunting term for a hound running backwards on the scent, yet 'draws dry foot' means tracking unerringly by the footprint — a sergeant who runs the wrong way still catches you.
detail: The cluster of hunting terms applied to a bailiff was a standard comic technique: the sergeant as a hound that tracks debtors like game. 'Counter' had an additional legal pun: the Counter was the name of two London debtors' prisons (the Poultry Counter and the Wood Street Counter), so 'runs counter' simultaneously means hunts backwards and drives men into the Counter prison. 'Dry foot' (following a cold trail) distinguished the slow, methodical hound from the faster 'hot-scent' hound; both meanings reinforce the sergeant's relentless, unstoppable pursuit. The whole description is also a mistaken-identity joke: the sergeant arrested Antipholus of Syracuse thinking he was Antipholus of Ephesus, who actually owes the debt.

anchor_text: arrested on a band? Not on a band, but on a stronger thing; A chain, a chain
summary: Adriana asks whether her husband was arrested on a 'band' — a legal bond or written obligation, the standard Elizabethan word for a formal debt-instrument. Dromio corrects her: not a band (a piece of paper) but a chain — the gold chain the goldsmith Angelo gave to Antipholus of Syracuse by mistake, and for which Antipholus of Ephesus now stands accused of non-payment. The pun works because a band ties a man legally, while a chain ties him physically, and both words name what holds him.
detail: A 'band' (variant of 'bond') was the written guarantee signed by a debtor acknowledging money owed; the creditor Angelo has had Antipholus of Ephesus arrested for refusing to pay for the chain he claims he never received. The irony is total: Antipholus of Ephesus genuinely did not receive it — his Syracusan twin did. So the arrest turns on a chain that created a legal band without the Ephesian's knowledge or consent. Dromio's wordplay makes the confusion into a riddle: what is stronger than a legal bond? The physical object that caused the legal confusion in the first place.

anchor_text: It was two ere I left him, and now the clock strikes one. The hours come back
summary: Dromio spins a sustained comic conceit: the clock has gone backwards (from two to one) because Time itself is in debt and runs from the sergeant like any debtor — 'Time is a very bankrupt, and owes more than he's worth to season.' The hours retreat out of fear; Time is a thief who steals the hours by night and day; and being both a debtor and a criminal, Time has excellent reason to turn back when a sergeant appears. The passage builds on the central crisis (arrest for debt) by making even abstract Time subject to the same comic law.
detail: The conceit is the play's most extended piece of pure Dromio bravura. 'Worth to season' plays on 'season' as (1) the proper time, (2) to ripen or season. The proposition that Time 'comes stealing on by night and day' — a proverbial observation about time's imperceptible passing — is here made literal: Time is a thief and therefore subject to arrest. Adriana dismisses it ('how fondly dost thou reason') but Dromio's logic is mock-rigorous: if time cannot be trusted to flow forward, and if debtors run from sergeants, then the sergeant on the street outside explains why the clock has gone backward. The comedy exploits the fact that a clock striking one after striking two would genuinely make no sense — Dromio turns even his own confusion into a law-court argument.

anchor_text: imaginary wiles, And Lapland sorcerers inhabit here
summary: Antipholus of Syracuse cannot explain why strangers greet him by name, offer him gifts, and measure him for clothes: he concludes the whole city is run by magic. 'Lapland sorcerers' invokes the Elizabethan belief that Lapland (Scandinavia's far north) was the homeland of witches and weather-magicians. His fear of being 'transformed' by Ephesian witchcraft echoes the biblical reputation of Ephesus itself as a city of 'curious arts' and exorcists (Acts 19).
detail: Antipholus of Syracuse is the traveller: he arrived in Ephesus knowing no one, yet everyone here treats him as a familiar friend. His bewilderment is perfectly rational — he is being mistaken for his identical twin, Antipholus of Ephesus, a respected Ephesian resident — but he has no way to know that. The audience watches him attribute to Lapland sorcery what is simply farce-mechanics: wrong twin, right treatment. 'Lapland sorcerers' was a stock early-modern shorthand for the most extreme witchcraft imaginable; Renaissance writers regularly placed the most powerful witches at the world's northern edge. The irony is that the play's setting, Ephesus, had its own biblical reputation for magic: Acts 19 describes Paul burning the city's books of 'curious arts' and casting out spirits. Shakespeare shifts the action of Plautus's Menaechmi from Epidamnus to Ephesus precisely to layer classical slapstick over this biblical resonance.

anchor_text: bass-viol in a case of leather
summary: Dromio shifts to legal and musical puns on the arresting sergeant. He goes 'like a bass-viol in a case of leather' — a large stringed instrument in its leather cover, i.e. a man swathed in his leather coat. He 'gives them a sob and rests them': 'rest' means arrest. 'Suits of durance' means hard-wearing prison clothes but also lawsuits that last; 'sets up his rest' means stakes everything (a gaming term); and the sergeant's 'mace' (his staff of office) is likened to a 'morris-pike,' a long battle-lance, mocking how grandly he wields a mere stick.
detail: Dromio's comic method here is sustained punning on the vocabulary of legal arrest. 'Rest' = arrest was a standing pun; 'durance' meant both prison and hard-wearing cloth ('suits of durance' are prison garments but also the lawsuit/warrant that puts you there). 'Sets up his rest' is from primero, a card game, meaning to risk one's whole stake on a single play — so the sergeant's entire purpose in life is to use that mace. 'Morris-pike' (Moorish pike) was a long lance, invoking the absurd martial gravity with which a debt-collector wields his ceremonial staff. The bass-viol simile also works bawdily — a large instrument in its leather case — though the main tenor is comic deflation: a man made entirely of noise and leather.

anchor_text: bark Expedition put forth to-night
summary: Dromio personifies the two ships as allegorical figures: the bark 'Expedition' (promptness) has already sailed, so they must wait for the 'hoy Delay' — a small slow coastal vessel named Delay. 'Angels' in the next line are gold coins (English angels, worth about ten shillings), not supernatural beings — Dromio has brought the ransom money, not divine messengers.

A 'hoy' was a small coastal trading vessel, slow and unimpressive — the perfect name for procrastination. The allegorical naming of ships (Expedition, Delay) is a Renaissance rhetorical device, personifying abstract qualities.

anchor_text: Satan, avoid! I charge thee, tempt me not
summary: When the Courtesan enters cheerfully asking about the chain he 'promised' her, Antipholus of Syracuse — who has never met her — thinks she must be a demon sent to trap him. 'Avoid' is the language of formal exorcism, echoing Christ's rebuke to Satan in the wilderness: 'Get thee behind me, Satan' (Matthew 4:10). His horror makes perfect farcical sense: to him, a strange woman who knows his name and claims he owes her valuables can only be supernatural. The audience knows she is addressing the wrong Antipholus — it is his Ephesian twin who dined with her and promised the chain.
detail: The Courtesan has a legitimate complaint: Antipholus of Ephesus dined at her house in a temper after being locked out of his own home, borrowed her ring, and promised in exchange the gold chain he was expecting from the goldsmith Angelo. Now she sees who she thinks is that same Antipholus, wearing a chain (in fact delivered to his Syracusan twin by mistake), and asks for it. The Syracusan, who knows nothing of any of this, interprets her confident familiarity as demonic knowledge — how else would a stranger know his name, know about a chain, claim a ring? 'Avoid' (from the Latin exorcism formula) and 'I charge thee' are the language of formal spirit-dismissal, the same diction used by exorcists in the chapels Elizabethans would have known from Catholic practice and from biblical accounts (Matthew 4:10; Mark 1:25).

anchor_text: devil's dam; and here she comes in the habit of a light wench
summary: Dromio insists the Courtesan is not Satan but worse: 'the devil's dam' (the devil's mother). She comes 'in the habit of a light wench' — wearing the clothes of a promiscuous woman — and 'light' triggers a rapid pun-chain: wenches who are 'light' (immoral) also give off light (like fire); 'It is written they appear to men like angels of light' (2 Corinthians 11:14 on Satan disguising himself as an angel); fire burns; therefore light wenches will burn — burn in hell, and also burn their partners with venereal disease.

'Dam' meaning mother (used of animals, especially mares) was a standard colloquial term; calling the Courtesan worse than Satan by being his mother is an escalation for comic effect. The string of reasoning — light/fire/burn — is a parody of academic logic, capped with the practical warning 'come not near her.' Elizabethan audiences would recognize 'burn' simultaneously as hellfire and syphilis.

anchor_text: he must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil
summary: When the Courtesan invites Antipholus to dine with her, Dromio warns his master via a well-known proverb: 'he must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil.' A long spoon lets you share a table with a dangerous companion while keeping your distance. The proverb warns that to have any dealings with someone wicked — to accept her hospitality, take her ring, or compromise with her demands — is to risk being drawn into her power.
detail: The proverb was proverbially old even by Shakespeare's day; it appears in Chaucer (The Squire's Tale, 'For he moot haue a long spoon that shal ete with the feend'). Shakespeare uses it again in The Tempest (2.2), where Stephano encounters Caliban and Trinculo, suggesting it was a stock comic saying. The comedy here is that Antipholus and Dromio are deadly serious — they genuinely believe the Courtesan is diabolical — while the audience knows she is an entirely ordinary woman with a legitimate financial grievance.

anchor_text: devils ask but the paring of one's nail, A rush, a hair, a drop of blood
summary: Dromio invokes Elizabethan folklore about making deals with the devil: minor spirits demand only trivial pledges — a nail paring, a rush, a hair, a drop of blood, a pin, a nut, a cherry-stone — in exchange for their service. That this Courtesan demands an actual gold chain makes her worse than ordinary demons, and Dromio warns that if given it, 'the devil will shake her chain, and fright us with it.'
detail: The list of trivial tokens — nail clippings, hair, blood, pins — reflects widely-circulated early-modern demonology: witchcraft pamphlets and contemporary sources such as Reginald Scot's The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) describe witches giving the devil their blood or hair as a compact. The penny-ante quality of these tokens makes the usual devil-bargain cheap; the Courtesan's greed for an actual gold chain elevates her threat. The final image — a devil shaking a chain — inverts the normal picture (the devil chains the damned) into a rattling threat. The chain itself has been the comedy's MacGuffin since Act 3: made for Antipholus of Ephesus but given to his Syracusan twin, it is now claimed by the Courtesan as a substitute for her ring, and will eventually land Antipholus of Ephesus in the debt-arrest already staged in the previous scene.

anchor_text: when I am cold he heats me with beating; when I am warm he cools me with beating
summary: Dromio builds a comic catalogue using a device called antithesis — a repeated pattern of opposites. anchor_text: Good Doctor Pinch, you are a conjurer
summary: Adriana calls Doctor Pinch a 'conjurer' — someone who commands spirits — and he immediately performs a formal exorcism, charging 'Satan' to leave Antipholus and yield to 'holy prayers.' In Shakespeare's England, learned men called 'conjurers' (and charlatans posing as them) claimed to bind and expel devils through Latin formulae and prayer. Pinch is both a schoolmaster and a quack exorcist; Ephesus, the city of Acts 19, was the biblical setting for just this kind of failed spiritual competition.

Professional exorcists — some Catholic priests, some self-styled Protestant healers — conducted public dispossessions that were highly theatrical and controversial. Samuel Harsnett attacked them in A Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures (1603), which Shakespeare also drew on for the devils in King Lear. The Ephesus setting reinforces the joke: Acts 19 describes the seven sons of Sceva attempting (and failing) to exorcise in the name of Jesus, and being beaten naked from the house by the demon — a comic precursor of what Pinch is about to experience.

summary: 'Ecstasy' here does not mean joy or delight. anchor_text: the fellow finds his vein, And, yielding to him, humours well his frenzy
summary: Doctor Pinch advises Adriana not to contradict Antipholus: 'the fellow finds his vein' means Dromio has hit on the right strategy by playing along. 'Vein' means a person's natural bent or mood; 'humours his frenzy' draws on the medical theory of the four humours — the belief that the body's four fluids (blood, phlegm, choler, melancholy) governed personality and illness. To 'humour' someone was to indulge their dominant fluid and so avoid agitating them.

A 'frenzy' (a violent mental disturbance) was attributed to overheated blood or choler; the therapeutic advice to avoid contradiction and 'yield' to the patient's mood was standard. The comedy here is that Pinch delivers this as sound medical science while himself about to bundle the innocent Antipholus into a dark room.

anchor_text: both man and master is possess'd; I know it by their pale and deadly looks: They must be bound, and laid in some dark room
summary: Binding a person believed to be mad or possessed and confining them in a dark room was the standard Elizabethan treatment for serious mental disturbance. Darkness was thought to calm the agitated mind, and restraint prevented harm. The diagnosis 'possess'd' (demonically possessed) led directly to this treatment, which is here farcical because both men are perfectly sane — they are simply telling the truth and being disbelieved.

Physicians like Timothy Bright (Treatise of Melancholie, 1586) and theologians argued about whether 'frenzy' was a bodily or a spiritual ailment, and Pinch as a schoolmaster-conjurer embodies exactly that confusion.

anchor_text: this grained face of mine be hid / In sap-consuming winter's drizzled snow, / And all the conduits of my blood froze up, / Yet hath my night of life some memory, / My wasting lamps some fading glimmer left
summary: Aegeon uses a chain of sustained metaphors for old age: 'grained' face = deeply furrowed (grain = the wood-grain of wrinkles); 'winter's drizzled snow' = white hair or beard covering his face; 'conduits of my blood froze up' = veins grown cold and sluggish with age; 'my night of life' = the darkness of old age; 'wasting lamps' = eyes that are dimming, like candles burning down. The whole passage treats the human body as a landscape at the end of its seasons.
detail: This speech is one of the few passages in Comedy of Errors that asks the audience to feel genuine sympathy rather than laughter. Aegeon's figurative language — borrowed partly from the Sonnets tradition of Time devouring the body — sets up the emotional release of his reunion with Emilia. 'Conduits' for blood-vessels was a commonplace anatomical metaphor in the period.

anchor_text: One of these men is genius to the other; / And so of these. Which is the natural man, / And which the spirit?
summary: A 'genius' in Roman belief was a man's attendant spirit — a divine double that accompanied each person through life. The Duke's bewildered question treats one Antipholus as real and the other as a ghostly counterpart or double. 'Natural man' means the actual flesh-and-blood human, as opposed to a spirit or demon in his likeness.
detail: The genius was a specifically Roman concept: every man had a personal genius, a kind of divine double that embodied his vitality and was worshipped on his birthday. The word later broadened to mean an attendant spirit more generally. The Duke's use of it here is both classically learned and dramatically apt: facing two men who are indistinguishable, the only rational explanation he can reach is that one is supernatural. The question 'which is the natural man, and which the spirit?' recasts the comedy's central trick as a metaphysical puzzle. In Plautus's Amphitruo — the other main source play — the 'double' of Amphitryon is actually the god Jupiter in disguise, so the genius question has a Plautine echo.

anchor_text: Whoever bound him, I will loose his bonds, / And gain a husband by his liberty
summary: The Abbess announces she will free Aegeon and — in the same breath — that she will 'gain a husband.' The audience has not yet been told who she is, but this line is the signal: Aegeon is her lost husband. This is the play's main anagnorisis (recognition), the moment the play's opening tragedy — the condemned old man separated from wife and family by shipwreck — is resolved in the same scene that closes the comedy.

anchor_text: By men of Epidamnum, he and I, / And the twin Dromio, all were taken up
summary: Emilia fills in the gap from Act 1: after the shipwreck, she, Antipholus of Syracuse (the baby), and one Dromio twin were picked up by sailors from Epidamnum; then Corinthian fishermen forcibly seized her son and that Dromio, leaving her stranded with the Epidamnians. This explains how Antipholus of Syracuse grew up in Syracuse with Aegeon while the other twin ended up in Ephesus.
detail: In Plautus's Menaechmi the original city in which the separated twins end up is Epidamnum (modern Durazzo, Albania), and Shakespeare preserves the name here. The play shifts Plautus's single-city setting to Ephesus for the theological resonance of that city in Acts 19 and Ephesians, but the Epidamnum reference survives as the original point of separation. The account finally reconciles the backstory Aegeon told at the play's opening, explaining why both twins ended up raised by separate families — one in Syracuse, one (via Corinthian fishermen) eventually in Ephesus.

anchor_text: Twenty-five years have I but gone in travail / Of you, my sons; nor till this present hour / My heavy burdens are delivered
summary: Emilia plays on the double meaning of 'travail' (hard labour; and also 'travel,' the journey through life) and 'delivered' (set free from a burden; and also 'to give birth'). She has been in labour for twenty-five years with these sons she could not deliver — now, at this moment, she gives birth to them a second time by recognizing and reuniting with them. 'Burdens' continues the childbirth metaphor.
detail: In Shakespeare's English 'travail' and 'travel' were nearly interchangeable in spelling and pronunciation, and 'deliver' covered both 'to free' and 'to bring forth a child.' The speech is the play's most sustained piece of structural wordplay: Emilia reframes the entire 25-year tragedy as a prolonged pregnancy, and this public square as her delivery room. The image of the re-birth of the family is both comic in its cheekiness and genuinely moving after the long opening scene of Aegeon's condemned captivity.

anchor_text: you the calendars of their nativity, / Go to a gossips' feast
summary: 'Calendars of their nativity' means the Dromio twins, whose own births mark the same day as the Antipholus twins — they are living records (calendars) of that birth date. 'Gossips' feast' is a christening party or baptismal celebration — guests at a christening were 'gossips' (god-parents and close friends), and the feast followed the ceremony. Emilia invites everyone to celebrate the family reunion as a second christening.

anchor_text: Methinks you are my glass, and not my brother: / I see by you I am a sweet-faced youth
summary: Dromio of Ephesus says to his twin: looking at you is like looking in a mirror ('glass'). Since they are identical, seeing the other Dromio is the first time he has ever seen his own face accurately reflected back at him. He concludes from the mirror-image that he must be handsome — with comic self-satisfaction.

anchor_text: We'll draw cuts for the senior: till then, lead thou first
summary: 'Draw cuts' means to draw lots by pulling straws of different lengths — the person who drew the short straw (or 'cut') lost. The Dromios cannot tell which of them is the elder twin, so they propose to settle who leads by chance. The play ends with neither twin going first: they go 'hand in hand, not one before another' — a final comic image of the equality that was always there, obscured by the day's errors.
detail: The Dromios' closing exchange is a model of comic resolution: the question of who is senior (the kind of birth-order, precedence, and rank question that obsesses the play's masters) is answered by refusing the question entirely. They go hand in hand — a visual emblem of the twins restored to each other, and an image of marriage too, since it echoes the hand-joining of the wedding ceremony. The whole final sequence of the Dromios after their masters exit is unique to Shakespeare and has no parallel in Plautus; it is the warmest moment in the play.
